item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Durante más de tres meses, los Yankees de Nueva York han planificado el regreso de Aaron Judge en torno a una idea: recuperar a su capitán para octubre sin exigirle que recupere de golpe los 99 días que se ha perdido.
Por eso su primera semana tras el regreso nunca pareció normal. Judge volvió sin haber pasado por una etapa de rehabilitación en las ligas menores. Los Yankees limitaron sus entradas, intercalaron descansos programados y consideraron los partidos de las Grandes Ligas como la fase final de su preparación. Solo jugó seis entradas en su regreso el 8 de septiembre y el martes tuvo un descanso programado tras disputar seis partidos seguidos.
Los Yankees estaban dispuestos a sacrificar el ritmo de septiembre a cambio de la forma física en octubre. Para este fin de semana en Arizona, se suponía que esa ecuación iba a cambiar. Judge ya había superado la fase de entrenamiento controlado. Nueva York se preparaba para aumentar su carga de trabajo y darle esos turnos al bate regulares que se había perdido durante su larga recuperación en la liga mayor.
La urgencia ya se notaba en los resultados. Judge tenía un promedio de 4 de 21 con 11 strikeouts en sus primeros seis partidos tras su reincorporación. Su jonrón de tres carreras del lunes en Minnesota fue la primera señal de que estaba dando la talla, pero no borró todos esos swings fallidos. Los Yankees necesitaban más práctica que otro reinicio.
Según la clasificación de la MLB, los Yankees tienen un balance de 88-64 al comenzar el viernes, a cinco partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con 10 partidos por disputar. Cuatro de ellos serán contra los Rays la semana que viene. La plaza para la postemporada está asegurada, pero Nueva York todavía tiene que prepararse para la lucha por el título de división y una posible serie de comodines.
Por eso, esta etapa no se centró tanto en demostrar que Judge podía volver, sino más bien en asegurarse de que pudiera volver a asumir la carga de trabajo habitual de octubre. Se suponía que cada partido le acercaría un poco más a su máximo rendimiento, le ayudaría a recuperar la sincronización frente a los lanzadores de las Grandes Ligas y eliminaría otra incertidumbre de cara a la postemporada. Se suponía que esa iba a ser la fase final y sin complicaciones del plan de los Yankees para octubre, antes de que empezara la postemporada.
El plan de puesta en marcha se ve interrumpido
En cambio, Judge llega a Arizona con una molestia en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha tras la derrota del miércoles por 5-4, en la 13.ª entrada, ante los Minnesota Twins en el Target Field. Notó el problema por primera vez en la primera entrada y siguió en el campo hasta que Heliot Ramos entró como bateador suplente en su lugar en la sexta.
Era su séptimo partido desde que volvió tras una fractura por estrés en la costilla derecha, después de 99 días de baja. Con esos dos strikeouts, su promedio desde que volvió queda en 4 de 23, con 13 strikeouts y un jonrón.
Judge dijo que intentó seguir jugando antes de que él y el entrenador Aaron Boone decidieran que el riesgo para los Yankees era mayor que lo que valía seguir en el campo.
«Intenté seguir jugando a ver hasta dónde podía llegar, porque estos partidos son importantes en esta recta final», dijo Judge. «Lo hablé con los míos y pensamos que sería lo mejor para no perjudicar al equipo, ni en el campo ni en las bases».
Los Yankees tuvieron el jueves libre para someterse a tratamiento. A primera hora del viernes, la MLB seguía indicando que tenía una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha, sin fecha de regreso.
David Cone señala un problema aún mayor para octubre
La primera cuestión es la disponibilidad. La más importante es la preparación.
El analista de YES Network, David Cone, se centró en eso el jueves. Judge ha tenido 24 turnos al bate desde que volvió, y 13 de ellos han acabado en strikeouts.
«Estoy preocupado», dijo Cone. «Necesita turnos al bate… Tiene un problema en la parte inferior de la pierna, en la pantorrilla. Simplemente no lo sabemos. No lo sabremos hasta que sepamos qué tan grave es. ¿Va a tener más turnos al bate antes de que acabe la temporada regular? Ahora mismo es una auténtica incógnita».
Ahora, el hecho de haberse saltado la fase de rehabilitación cobra más importancia. El exreceptor All-Star A.J. Pierzynski dijo que una temporada en las ligas menores podría haberle proporcionado un entorno menos exigente para lidiar con las molestias tras una larga ausencia.
«Por eso te vas de rehabilitación, sobre todo cuando has estado tanto tiempo de baja como Aaron Judge. Él mismo lo ha dicho: esto es como los entrenamientos de primavera, así que intentas quitarte de encima las molestias y otras cosillas que surgen yendo de rehabilitación», dijo Pierzynski. «Él no lo hizo, no quiso hacerlo».
Nadie puede saber si una asignación a la rehabilitación habría evitado esa tensión en la pierna. Los Yankees ahora corren el riesgo de que Judge pierda más turnos al bate que aún necesita.
El equilibrio de los pelotones no es el problema
Una comparación actual del OPS de los Yankees y los Red Sox destaca a Judge, Ben Rice y Cody Bellinger como bateadores de Nueva York que rinden bien contra cualquiera de los dos equipos. Según Baseball Savant, Judge tiene un OPS de 0,839 contra lanzadores diestros y de 0,892 contra zurdos. Bellinger tiene unas cifras casi idénticas: 0,794 y 0,795. Rice tiene un OPS de 0,937 contra lanzadores diestros y de 0,784 contra zurdos.
Judge no necesita un papel de bateador de reserva. Los Yankees necesitan que esté listo para batear regularmente contra cualquier rival.
Judge tiene un promedio de bateo de .241/.360/.511, con 18 jonrones y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos. La cuestión es si los Yankees podrán recuperar el ritmo de juego suficiente antes de octubre.
El plazo de la Liga Internacional convierte la precaución en una apuesta con la plantilla
Si los Yankees metieran a Judge en la lista de lesionados ahora, no podría jugar hasta el partido 161, lo que le dejaría, como mucho, el último partido de la temporada regular para ponerse a punto.
Si los Yankees creen que puede volver antes, pueden mantenerlo en la plantilla y jugar temporalmente con un jugador menos disponible en la plantilla de 28.
Jasson Domínguez y Max Schuemann figuraban ambos en la alineación del equipo de Triple A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre el jueves, lo que sugiere que no habrá ningún sustituto inmediato.
Esto deja a Nueva York ante la disyuntiva que intentó evitar durante el primer regreso de Judge: proteger su físico o proteger su preparación. A falta de 10 partidos, puede que los Yankees no tengan tiempo suficiente para hacer ambas cosas a fondo.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Aaron Judge already was running out of time to nail down his timing before the playoffs began.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Now, a tight lower right leg threatens to disrupt that further, if not have more serious ramifications for his availability down the road.
For now, the Yankees were hoping Thursday’s off day, during which Judge was expected to receive more treatment on his leg, would be well-timed.
His status beyond that, though, was still a question mark as they entered Friday’s series opener against the Diamondbacks.
That the next three games are on turf is not ideal, given that the Yankees are often cautious using players who are dealing with any kind of soft-tissue leg injury on the artificial surface.
It is possible the Yankees use the weekend to make sure Judge gets healthy before deploying him for Tuesday’s showdown against the Rays, who now lead the American League East by five games with 10 to play.
While this weekend’s games are important in that race, the Yankees much rather would ensure Judge is ready for the playoffs instead of potentially making the injury worse by playing him in hopes of chasing down the Rays for the division.
In a hint of potential good news — or perhaps just avoiding the worst-case scenario — both Jasson Domínguez and Max Schuemann were in the lineup Thursday night at Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, suggesting the Yankees at least were not immediately calling up an injury replacement for Judge, though that does not preclude them from doing so in the coming days.
But if the Yankees believe Judge has a chance to play again before the regular season is over, it is unlikely he will go back on the injured list because doing so would keep him out through Game 161.
So if they have to play a man short over the next few days, they will, especially with rosters already expanded.
Before leaving Wednesday’s game against the Twins in the sixth inning, Judge was batting only 4-for-23 (.174) with a .513 OPS and one home run in his first seven games back from missing three-plus months with a right rib stress fracture.
After the Yankees had eased him back in, he essentially was expected to be a full go starting Friday, meaning plenty of consistent at-bats to get locked in, at least until the leg tightness popped up.
“I feel like you deal with this every spring training,” Judge said Wednesday. “Usually start of the season once you start ramping up again, things pop up and that’s where we’ve been — thankfully this whole time coming back, nothing’s really nagged us. So hopefully, it’s just one little thing and we’re back out there soon.”

The New York Yankees are headed to the MLB playoffs! But they have a lot to figure out before they *likely* have to face the Boston Red Sox in a 3-game Wild Card series.
A big storyline surrounding the Yankees right now is what manager Aaron Boone will do with Anthony Volpe when Jazz Chisholm Jr. returns.
Since Jazz went to the IL (and Volpe was called up). Volpe has had his fair share of moments, and it begs the question: What will the Yankees' infield layout look like?
Yankees fans may hate to admit it, but with Volpe's previous playoff experience, it might be wise to give the kid a shot in October.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Predicted to 'Dump' Luis Gil Ahead of Playoffs
What Should the Yankees Do with Anthony Volpe?
Has Anthony Volpe done enough to remain on the Yankees roster? Should be play second or third base in the MLB playoffs in place of Jazz Chisholm Jr. or Ryan McMahon.
Over his last seven games, Anthony Volpe has a home run, two doubles, eight hits, 7 RBI, and scored three runs.
In all likelihood, Jazz still has his 2B spot when he returns, but Ryan McMahon?? That's another question.
Ryan McMahon’s career numbers with the Yankees:
🤮 171 G🤮 .212 AVG🤮 14 HR🤮 52 RBI🤮 .636 OPS
How would you grade McMahon’s time in pinstripes so far? pic.twitter.com/cVEPiw5FFF
— SleeperYankees (@SleeperYankees) September 17, 2026
What will Volpe's role be when Jazz comes back?
Second baseman Anthony Volpe (7 games).348 BA // 1 HR // 7 RBI // .400 OBP // .965 OPS#Yankees pic.twitter.com/cqwisk1tw7
— Fireside Yankees (@FiresideYankees) September 17, 2026
Ryan McMahon is batting .210 this season with 10 home runs, 34 RBI, and just 66 hits.
And half of his games are in a hitters' haven for lefties.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Get Strong Jasson Dominguez Message Ahead of MLB Playoffs
Anthony Volpe's 2026 Season at a Glance
While Anthony Volpe's 2026 stats don't light the world on fire, it's fair to note he hasn't been given an extended runway to make a major impact, as he's bounced between AAA and the Bigs frequently.
Across 63 games this season, Volpe is batting .253 (career-high) with 14 XBH, 26 RBI, and an OPS+ of 92 (also would be career-high).
He's cut down on some of the strikeouts, and is still working a decent amount of walks.
Yankees fans, let me know in the comments what you think Anthony Volpe's role should be with the team in October?
If it were me (and being clear, I'm not the GM!) I'd run Volpe out there in October at 3B. It gives the lineup right-left balance, and Anthony Volpe has at least shown a capability of putting the ball in play that Ryan McMahon hasn't.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are officially IN the MLB playoff picture, as they recently clinched a postseason berth.
While the Yankees still have a small percentage chance to win the AL East, they will likely be in the AL Wild Card round, playing the Boston Red Sox.
In such a big series, decisions will have to be made regarding who gets a 26-man roster spot.
One player who is on the outside looking in and will likely be left off is Luis Gil.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Get Strong Jasson Dominguez Message Ahead of MLB Playoffs
Yankees Urged to Leave Luis Gil Off Playoff Roster
Recently, FanSided.com writer Jake Elman predicted a handful of players who will be 'dumped' from the playoff roster, or essentially dumped from the 26-man fold.
"But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don't expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. Clarke Schmidt's return gives the Yankees another depth arm, and Gil hasn't shown that he's worth carrying on a limited staff. That said, we imagine he'd be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates. "
Gil has pitched just 23.1 innings for the Yankees this season, and carries a 5.40 ERA in that span.
So, yeah, it's fair to assume his spot on the playoff roster may not be safe.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision
What Has Luis Gil Done in His MLB Career
Luis Gil has technically pitched in five seasons with the New York Yankees.
He briefly pitched in 2021 and 2022 with the club, but did not pitch at all in MLB in 2023 before bursting onto the scene in 2024 (AL Rookie of the Year).
However, since earning that top accolade, he has not been consistent as a member in the Yankees rotation.
Across 265.1 total IP in his career, Gil holds a very respectable 3.66 ERA, but perhaps his absence from the Bigs is a product of the Yankees' loaded rotation, rather than his individual ability.

The New York Yankees have lots of decisions to make ahead of their pursuit for a World Series crown.
After the Yankees clinched a postseason berth recently, as expected, it’s time to start thinking about who the Yankees could roll out in their 26-man October roster.
One fringe player is outfielder Jasson Dominguez, and recently, FanSided.com’s Jake Elman sent a strong message regarding Dominguez’s roster chances.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision
Will Jasson Dominguez Make Yankees Playoff Roster?
Right now, for the Yankees, the biggest storyline on the postseason roster front is Aaron Judge.
Judge has noted that he’s healthy after exiting a recent game against the Twins, but he’s the Yankees’ crown jewel.
Anywho, back to Jasson Dominguez, who is 100% a fringe roster candidate headed into October.
Elman recently noted Dominguez as a player who may be dumped from the Yankees’ postseason roster, and he wrote:
“The writing has long been on the wall for Domínguez, who was recently demoted to Triple-A amid another disappointing season. Even if Judge potentially misses the Wild Card Round, it’s difficult to envision the 23-year-old Domínguez returning as a backup outfielder. Frankly, the entire situation is unfortunate, because neither Domínguez’s talent nor his work ethic has been the issue. He’s always earned rave reviews for his maturity and overall attitude, but injuries — most notably to his elbow and shoulder — have seemingly sapped him of his once-potent power stroke.”
More MLB on Heavy: Former Chicago Cubs Player Demoted by New MLB Team
Jasson Dominguez’s 2026 Season
Jasson Dominguez was expected to take a leap in his development this season as the Yankees’ top backup outfielder, but he’s bounced back between the Bigs and minors all season due to inconsistent performance up in the big leagues.
Across 57 games played this season, Dominguez has batted just .225 with a negative bWAR, six home runs, 12 doubles, and an OPS+ of 75.
Those statistics aren’t very good.
Yankees fans, what would you do with Jasson Dominguez as the MLB playoffs approach? Would he be on your roster as a backup outfielder/pinch-runner?

item.content:encoded:
For their sake, the New York Yankees better hope that superstar outfielder Aaron Judge’s newest injury is only a minor setback.
Judge left Wednesday’s extra-inning loss to the Twins with lower leg tightness, immediately raising concerns among fans that he’ll miss the Yankees’ first playoff series. New York entered play on Sept. 17 in firm control of the AL’s top Wild Card seed, putting them on track to host the No. 5 Red Sox in the first round.
If Judge can’t go when the playoffs begin on Sept. 29, then he won’t be the only notable contributor not in uniform during the Wild Card Series. Each team gets 26 players for their playoff rosters, but no more than 13 pitchers. Some clubs opt for 14 position players and 12 pitchers, though we personally prefer a 13-and-13 balance. Additionally, teams can adjust their rosters between series, and obviously they can replace an injured player if needed.
For this list, we’re only including players who are healthy and active as of Sept. 17. In other words, that means Trent Grisham, Giancarlo Stanton, and Ryan Weathers are among those who didn’t qualify. We’ve also omitted Judge because the Yankees haven’t announced the severity of his left leg injury.
Jasson Domínguez, OF
The writing has long been on the wall for Domínguez, who was recently demoted to Triple-A amid another disappointing season. Even if Judge potentially misses the Wild Card Round, it’s difficult to envision the 23-year-old Domínguez returning as a backup outfielder.
Frankly, the entire situation is unfortunate, because neither Domínguez’s talent nor his work ethic has been the issue. He’s always earned rave reviews for his maturity and overall attitude, but injuries — most notably to his elbow and shoulder — have seemingly sapped him of his once-potent power stroke.
Luis Gil, P
Gil has had an odd career, winning AL Rookie of the Year in 2024 despite debuting three years earlier. Injuries have limited him to a 3.92 ERA over 80.1 innings since the start of 2025, and he recently moved to the bullpen. We’ll see whether the Yankees view the 28-year-old as a long-term reliever, or if they’d bring him to spring training as a starter.
But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don’t expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. Clarke Schmidt’s return gives the Yankees another depth arm, and Gil hasn’t shown that he’s worth carrying on a limited staff. That said, we imagine he’d be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates.
Paul Goldschmidt, 1B/DH
Goldschmidt turned 39 last week, and it’s unclear whether he’s in the final weeks of a likely Hall of Fame career. He’s totaled 65.3 bWAR, and the majority of the 142 players above him are already in the Hall of Fame or will be when they’re eligible.
Let’s get back to the present. Goldschmidt is hitting just .239 with a .680 OPS in 103 second-half plate appearances, and he’s only capable of playing first or DHing. Ben Rice fills both roles, and Cody Bellinger can also play first if needed.
The one thing potentially working in Goldschmidt’s favor is his .313 average and 1.006 OPS against lefties, but that’s not enough to warrant a roster spot in our eyes. Sorry, Goldy. At least you’d finally earn a World Series ring if the Yankees finish the job.
Will Warren, SP
This might come as a surprise, given that we included Warren in our most recent playoff roster projection. But the more that we think about things, Schmidt’s return feels like a significant blow to Warren’s chances of pitching in October. Do the Yankees really need two long relievers capable of eating up innings if the starter leaves early?
We initially had veteran swingman Ryan Yarbrough in this spot, though he might have the advantage as a left-handed reliever.. He also has a 2.91 ERA in 21.2 second-half innings and has since recovered from a lingering right oblique problem.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

item.content:encoded:
MINNESOTA — Aaron Judge’s health has the Yankees holding their breath once again.
The slugger left Wednesday’s 5-4, 13-inning loss to the Twins prematurely when Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him with a runner on and one out in the top of the sixth inning. The Yankees were only down two runs at the time, and Judge, initially expected to rest on Wednesday, was fresh off an off day.
A short time later, the Yankees announced that Judge exited the game with tightness in his right lower leg. The news comes with the right fielder just seven games removed from a 99-day absence for a stress fracture in his first right rib.
“Hopefully, it’s something we were able to catch,” Aaron Boone said after the game.
Neither Boone nor Judge specified what part of the body the latter hurt. Judge, always unrevealing when it comes to his injuries, wouldn’t even say it was his leg, stating he simply had a “lower body” issue.
Judge did say that he first felt something while playing the field in the first inning on Wednesday, but he couldn’t pinpoint a particular play. Boone said he no knowledge of an injury prior to Wednesday, and that he wasn’t made aware of the problem until he noticed Judge hobbling in the outfield on a play he wasn’t involved in during the bottom of the fifth inning.
Judge also appeared to grimace when he took a check swing on the first pitch of his third-inning at-bat.
“I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said. “But in talking it over, I thought it’d be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team in the field or on the basepaths.
“I didn’t think it was smart to push it too much here.”
There is no update on Aaron Judge as of this moment
🎥: @YESNetwork pic.twitter.com/hifw6hg9W5
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) September 16, 2026
Judge is facing his latest injury scare with just 10 games left in the regular season. The Yankees have the day off on Thursday before beginning a three-game series at Arizona’s Chase Field, a turfed surface that wouldn’t be friendly to a lower body injury. The second-place Yanks, who have already secured a playoff berth, will then host a crucial four-game series against the division-leading Rays from Sept. 22-24.
With the off day on Thursday, the Yankees will see how Judge responds to treatment. He said “I don’t know” and “probably not” when asked if he’ll get testing, though Boone wasn’t sure about that.
“Hopefully it’s just one little thing,” Judge said, “and then we’re back out there soon.”
Judge likened his leg issue to the types of nagging injuries that pop up during spring training and at the start of the season when players are ramping up their bodies. He has been doing just that since returning from his rib injury on Sept. 8.
“We’re still trying to ramp up, so there’s going to be little things like this that come up,” Judge said. “I just thought it’d be best to — instead of pushing through it like I normally do, and it might become a little worse — get somebody who’s ready to go in there and just try and do what’s best for the team.”
It should be noted that Judge’s rib rehab and pre-activation build-up skipped some steps. He got his wish after repeatedly making it clear that he wanted to forego a minor league rehab assignment despite missing over three months. The superstar also only faced living pitching once, and that came against some minor leaguers.
Asked if Wednesday’s injury made him rethink the process, Judge told the Daily News, “People blow out their calves and blow out their quads in rehab assignments, so I don’t think taking a game in Double-A will change any of that.”
He added that he felt his build-up has been gradual, as he had felt asymptomatic for weeks before returning.
“That’s what we kind of did with playing the [seven] innings, playing the eight innings,” Judge said, referring to his planned early exits in his first two games back, the first of which he said he was “not happy” about the night of.
Judge also had off on Sept. 10.
Prior to Wednesday, Boone had said that he’s been “pleased” with the way Judge has been responding physically since returning to game action. Judge, who has said he wants to be playing every day, said much of the same over the weekend.
The captain, who went 0-for-2 with two strikeouts before departing on Wednesday, hasn’t had much success at the plate since coming off the injured list as he searches for his timing. He did crush a three-run homer in Monday’s victory over the Twins, but he entered that game 3-for-17 (.176) with zero extra-base hits in his first five games back.
Still, the Yankees have been thrilled to have Judge back in a lineup that struggled mightily without him. With Judge’s mere presence impacting the way those around him are attacked, the Bombers had one of the worst offenses in baseball while the back-to-back MVP was on the IL, ranking last in K% (26.1%); 29th in wRC+ (90) and average (.227); 28th in wOBA (.299); 27th in OPS (.681); and 24th in runs scored (341) from June 2 through Sept. 7.
“I’m not sure exactly what’s going on, but it’s never good when your best player on your team comes out of the lineup,” Carlos Rodón said after battling some velocity issues and tightness of his own on Wednesday. “So obviously, I’m hoping he’s gonna be okay. I’m not sure exactly what’s happening, but I’m sure he’ll be fine.”
While it’s too soon to know if Judge will miss extended time, the Yankees will have limited options for his roster spot if that’s the case. There’s fellow outfielder Jasson Domínguez, but he cannot be trusted to play defense in the critical games that are coming up.
Utilityman Max Schuemann is another choice at Triple-A who can also play the outfield.
Of course, the Yankees are hoping it doesn’t come to that.
“Obviously, he’s a key figure to what we do,” Boone said. “Hopefully, we get it treated and knock it out and [he can] be a factor at some point.”

item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday night, the New York Yankees and Minnesota Twins will play the second game of their series at Target Field.
The Yankees will be looking to build off an 8-3 win on Monday.
Bob Nightengale of USA Today wrote (during Monday’s game): “The New York Yankees now clinch a postseason berth with the Blue Jays’ defeat. The Yankees are up 7-3 over the Twins in the 9th, so the party will be in Minneapolis”
UPDATE: The Yankees won 8-1.
Yankees Announced Domínguez News
Earlier this month, the Yankees demoted Jasson Domínguez.
The Yankees wrote (via X) on September 10: “Following tonight’s game, the Yankees optioned OF Jasson Domínguez to Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre.”
The Yankees have now announced that Domínguez has reported to the RailRiders.
SWB RailRiders wrote (on September 15): “The Yankees have made the following roster moves affecting SWB: • C Edinson Durán placed on the Development List • OF Jasson Domínguez optioned by the Yankees and has reported to SWB”
Looking At Domínguez
Domínguez (who is 23) has already spent part of four seasons at the MLB level.
Despite being a notable prospect, he has had mixed results.
Before getting sent down, Domínguez had been batting .225 with 47 hits, six home runs, 14 RBIs, 22 runs and eight stolen bases in 57 games this year.
It will be interesting to see if Domínguez gets another chance with the Yankees this season.
There is also reason to speculate about his future with the franchise going forward.
Yankees Ahead Of Tuesday’s Game
The Yankees have had a very solid 2026 season.
They are the second-place team in the American League East with an 87-63 record in 150 games.
On the road, the Yankees have gone 45-31 in 76 games.
